name: The Streisand Effect
statement: Try to bury information and you dig it up for everyone to see.
meaning: The Streisand effect is the phenomenon in which an attempt to hide, remove, or censor a piece of information ends up publicising it far more widely, typically across the internet. The very act of suppression draws the attention it sought to avoid, turning an obscure item into a cause celebre.
mechanism: Censorship attracts attention through several channels. Being told something is off-limits sharpens the desire to see it, the psychological reactance of forbidden fruit. A lawsuit or takedown is itself a newsworthy event, whereas the obscure item was not. And once information is online, it can be copied, mirrored, and screenshotted faster than it can be removed, so the effort to erase it seeds the copies that outlive it.

examples.text: In 2003 Barbra Streisand sued a photographer over an aerial image of her Malibu home in a coastal-erosion archive, seeking fifty million dollars; before the suit the photo had been downloaded six times, two by her own lawyers, and afterward the site drew hundreds of thousands of visitors. The suit was dismissed and she was ordered to pay legal fees.

When a consortium sent takedown letters over an HD-DVD decryption key in 2007, the key spread to hundreds of thousands of web pages, and onto shirts and songs, precisely because of the attempt to suppress it.
Numerous cease-and-desist letters and takedown demands have amplified the very material they targeted, the general class of cases the term names.

variants.name: The selection-bias caveat
variants.text: The counterpoint that most suppression succeeds quietly and is never noticed precisely because it works, so the effect is what we see when censorship backfires, not a rule that it will.

variants.name: Reactance and forbidden fruit
variants.text: The psychological engine of the effect: being told information is off-limits increases the drive to seek it out.

whyItMatters: It has become the standard name for a real hazard of the internet age — that heavy-handed suppression can be self-defeating — and a caution routinely invoked by lawyers, public-relations advisers, and anyone weighing whether to demand that something be taken down. It captures how the architecture of the web can turn an act of control into an act of publicity.

working.text: before demanding that something be removed, ask whether the demand will draw more eyes than the thing itself ever would.
where possible, prefer low-key approaches to loud legal threats, which are themselves newsworthy.

working.lead: Do not assume it always fires
working.text: remember that plenty of suppression works unnoticed, so treat the effect as a risk, not a certainty.

limits: It is a named social and media pattern, not a quantified law, and above all not a guaranteed outcome. Censorship frequently does succeed: most takedowns and suppression efforts work quietly and are never noticed, precisely because success is invisible — a selection-bias point worth stating plainly. The effect is notable when suppression backfires, but there is no reliable rule that it will, and its reach depends on how newsworthy the attempt is and how easily the material can be copied. Even in the namesake case, the exact damages figure is reported inconsistently across sources.
misreadings: It is not a law that censorship always backfires; it is the memorable name for the cases where it does. The many quiet successes go unrecorded, so the effect can look more inevitable than it is. And it is a coined label for an observed pattern, not a discovered natural regularity.
origin: Coined by Mike Masnick of the technology blog Techdirt on 5 January 2005, naming the pattern after Barbra Streisand's 2003 lawsuit over an aerial photograph of her home, which drew vastly more attention to the image than it had ever had.

sources.text: Streisand effect, Wikipedia. — the definition, the 2003 lawsuit and download figures, the encryption-key case, and the coining by Masnick.
